text.text: National Institutes of Health (NIH) Diversity Supplements have the potential to address concerns regarding a lack of diversity and equity in psychological science.
However, while Diversity Supplements have been available for nearly all NIH research grants, they have been vastly underutilized.
This study sought to identify common barriers and facilitators to Diversity Supplement utilization among psychologists, in order to identify pathways towards increasing utilization.
Principal investigators on NIH grants between 2014-2022 were invited to participate in a one-time survey.

Respondents (N = 3,760 principal investigators, n = 690 psychologists) completed ad-hoc measures assessing rates of Diversity Supplement application and receipt, factors associated with each, and self-reported barriers to application.
Less than half of surveyed psychologists had ever applied for a Diversity Supplement.
Logistic regression analyses found that psychologists of racially minoritized identity and at advanced career stages were more likely to have applied for a Diversity Supplement.
Among psychologists who had not applied for a Diversity Supplement, the most common barriers were a lack of eligible mentees and confusion over eligibility criteria.
These barriers may be addressed via (a) the creation of an informal matching system(s) to match eligible trainees to PIs and (b) new and improved awareness campaigns regarding Diversity Supplements.

In 1989, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) introduced the Diversity Supplement, a new funding mechanism designed to address inequities in research funding by providing a new source of funding for scientists from underrepresented minority groups (National Institutes of Health, 1989).

text.text: Between 1989 and 2025, 1 the Diversity Supplement has provided funding for early-stage researchers to be mentored through existing NIH-funded research grants.

The goal of the program is to "improve the diversity of the research workforce by recruiting and supporting post-baccalaureate, predoctoral students, post-doctorates, and eligible early-stage investigators from groups that have been shown to be underrepresented in health-related research" (David et al., 2022).

text.text: As such, Diversity Supplements exist within a larger landscape of programs in the U.S. that aim to increase diversity in the health services research workforce.

text.text: As articulated by the Theoretical Domains Framework, "implementing new practices requires changes in the behaviour of relevant actors, and this is facilitated by understanding of the determinants of current and desired behaviours" (Atkins et al., 2017).

text.text: Any occurrence of a desired behavior can be broadly understood through three essential conditions: individuals must have the capability to perform the behavior, the opportunity to enact it, and the motivation to choose it.

The Theoretical Domains Framework provides a detailed, theory-driven, actionable breakdown of these broad categories, allowing researchers to identify specific psychological, contextual, and motivational barriers that can be targeted through intervention.

Thus, if the field aims to increase the use of NIH Diversity Supplements, it is important to leverage theoretical frameworks like Theoretical Domains Framework to understand the underlying determinants of researchers' behavior at a more granular level.
The Theoretical Domains Framework articulates factors that shape behavior in the context of "implementation problems" like the utilization of Diversity Supplements.

A number of domains have been identified, such as knowledge of a behavior (e.g., understanding how to do something), intentions of engaging in a behavior, beliefs about the consequences of engaging in a behavior, and the presence of reinforcers of a behavior (Atkins et al., 2017).

text.text: In the context of the present study, these domains contribute to researchers' capability, opportunity, and motivation to pursue Diversity Supplements.
Understanding these determinants provides a foundation for designing strategies to enhance engagement with this funding mechanism.
Present Study.
Diversity Supplements have the potential to increase equity in psychological research funding and in the psychological research workforce.
However, for this impact to be achieved, psychologists must successfully apply to, and receive, Diversity Supplements.
With this in mind, the authors conducted a survey of principal investigators (PIs) on NIH grants funded between 2014-2022 to answer the following research questions.
First, the authors assessed rates of Diversity Supplement application and receipt among psychologists, and compared these rates to those among non-psychologists.

Second, the authors examined the relationship between psychologist characteristics (e.g., years of experience) and Diversity Supplement application and receipt, with a goal of identifying which characteristics may serve as barriers or facilitators to receiving Diversity Supplements.
Lastly, the authors assessed the self-reported barriers that prevent some psychologists from applying for Diversity Supplements.
These analyses were exploratory in nature and did not have specific hypotheses.
Participants included N = 3,760 researchers who were listed as the contact PI on NIH-funded grants between 2014-2022.
PI emails were collected from the NIH Freedom of Information Act Office, which makes mailing and email addresses of NIH-supported PIs publicly available on their website.

The research team sent emails to each PI email address linked to an NIH-funded grant between 2014-2022 inviting the recipient to participate in the study, which was described in the subject line as "Diversity Supplement Survey" (see complete survey for informed consent form with longer description).

A total of 134,457 email invitations were sent, resulting in 4,540 complete or partial survey responses (a response rate of approximately 3.4%, although some email addresses were likely out of use by the time of our study).
The present study focuses on diversity supplement utilization among psychologist respondents (n = 690).
All study procedures were approved by the University of Pittsburgh institutional review board (STUDY23050201).
All participants provided consent electronically.
Participants were asked to complete a brief one-time online survey, administered via Qualtrics.

The survey included 8-13 items (the exact number of items varied based on whether or not the respondent had applied for and/or received a diversity supplement) and the median response time was 3.4 minutes.
The complete survey is available at https://osf.io/dx5j6/.

text.text: Out of the 4,540 responses collected, 3,760 (82.8%) were completed and included non-missing data regarding respondent discipline and experience with Diversity Supplements; these responses were included in the present study.
No other inclusion or exclusion criteria were applied.
Of the 3,760 study participants, 3,000 (79.8%) agreed to provide optional demographic information (e.g., age, gender, race, ethnicity, etc.).
All data were collected via a one-time Qualtrics survey, available at https://osf.io/dx5j6/.

text.text: Measures of PIs' experiences with Diversity Supplements were ad hoc and developed for the present study.

Respondents selected one of the following options to describe their experience with Diversity Supplement applications: "supported an application that was awarded," "supported an application that was NOT awarded," "never supported an application," or "started but did not finish."
Respondents who had not applied (the latter two options) went on to report on the barriers that prevented them from supporting an application.

Respondents selected from a list of barriers derived from the Theoretical Domains Framework, a set of constructs known to help or hinder the implementation of desired practices (https://paperpile.com/c/q2qUOa/2TAXW/?prefix=e.g.%2C%20%5Black%20of%5D%20knowledge%2C%20%5Black%20of%5D%20incentives%20or%20reinforcement%3B  Atkins et al., 2017).

Respondents who had applied (whether awarded or not) were asked a series of questions assessing overall number of Diversity Supplements supported as well as the type of grant and trainee involved with the application(s).
Respondents could choose from a list of disciplines or write their own.

Discipline was coded as psychology if a respondent chose one of "Behavioral Health," "Clinical Psychology," "Cognitive Psychology," "Social Psychology," or "Other Psychology" as their discipline, or if they chose "Other" and wrote in the word "psychology."

Discipline was coded as non-psychology if a respondent chose one of "Biology," "Chemistry," "Epidemiology," "Neuroscience," "Pharmacology," "Psychiatry," Virology," or chose "Other" and did not write in the word "psychology."
Respondents could opt-in to providing demographic information.

Demographic variables included age, gender (man, woman, trans/gender diverse), and race/ethnicity (American Indian/Alaska Native non-Hispanic, Asian non-Hispanic, Black non-Hispanic, Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander non-Hispanic, White non-Hispanic, multiple non-Hispanic, other non-Hispanic, and Hispanic).

Outside of discipline, the survey collected information on institution type (e.g., university, academic medical center), job title (e.g., associate professor, full professor), roles mentored (e.g., doctoral students, early career researchers) years of experience conducting grant-funded research, percent of time spent on research, and percent of salary supported by research funding (See Table 1 for full list of response options).

text.text: First, the authors assessed whether psychologists were more or less likely to apply for-or to receive-Diversity Supplements, when compared to non-psychologists.

The authors assessed this by reporting the frequency of Diversity Supplement application and receipt among psychologists and non-psychologists and used Chi-square tests of independence to compare frequencies across groups.
There was no missing data in this analysis, as respondents who did not provide data regarding their discipline or their experience with Diversity Supplements were excluded from the present study.

In line with assumptions regarding Chi-square tests, both variables were categorical, all observations were independent (i.e., each row represented a unique participant), and all expected frequencies were greater than five (McHugh, 2013).

text.text: Second, the authors assessed the relationship between different psychologist characteristics (age, gender, race, institution type, job title, research time, research funding, years of experience, and roles mentored) and (a) Diversity Supplement application and (b) Diversity Supplement receipt.
These relationships were tested using logistic regression, which estimates the effect of each predictor variable on the odds of the outcome occurring.

For each outcome, the authors estimated bivariate models (where each psychologist characteristic was examined on its own, and each odds ratio represents the effect of a given characteristic on the outcome without controlling for other characteristics) and combined models (where all psychologist characteristics were examined in the same model, and each odds ratio represents the effect of a given characteristic on the outcome after controlling for other characteristics).

Thus, the authors calculated four odds ratios per researcher characteristic: (1) the bivariate odds ratio on Diversity Supplement application, (2) the adjusted odds ratio on application, (3) the bivariate odds ratio on Diversity Supplement receipt, and (4) the adjusted odds ratio on receipt.
Missing data (respondents were not required to provide demographic information) were dropped on a model-by-model basis.
Furthermore, some variables were recoded in order for the regression models to be reliably fit.
For categorical independent variables, levels with fewer than n = 25 participants were either dropped or collapsed with similar categories to ensure that models could be fit reliably.

text.text: A total of 690 psychologists and 3,070 non-psychologists completed the survey.

Among psychologists, the majority of respondents reported being White non-Hispanic (67.4%; 80.0% of respondents who provided race/ethnicity data) and female (64.1%; 75.6% of respondents who provided gender data), with a mean age of 48.2 and an average of 16.7 years of experience conducting grant-funded research.
The most commonly reported subfields were behavioral health (46.2%), clinical psychology (36.2%), cognitive psychology (8.6%), social psychology (4.2%) and other psychological fields (4.8%).

Most psychologists reported working at either a university (41.3%) or an academic medical center (34.6%), and the majority reported being either full (32.5%), associate (23.3%), or assistant (16.1%) professors.
It was common for respondents to mentor individuals across a number of roles, including doctoral students (64.9%), undergraduate students (52.5%), and early career researchers (51.0%).
Psychologists reported spending an average of 70.3% of their time on research and having 64.8% of their salary supported by research activities.

Psychologists were no more or less likely to apply for (X 2 (1) = 2.06, p = .151) or to receive (X 2 (1) = 2.06, p = .151) a Diversity Supplement when compared to researchers in other fields.

In terms of Diversity Supplement applications, psychologists were more likely to apply for a Diversity Supplement (1) if they were Black non-Hispanic relative to White non-Hispanic (OR = 3.00, 95% CI: 1.23, 7.38); (2) if they were Hispanic relative to White non-Hispanic (OR = 2.67, 95% CI: 1.00, 7.14); (3) if they were a full professor relative to non-professor (OR = 2.32, 95% CI: 1.09, 5.06); (4) if they mentored post-baccalaureate researchers (OR = 1.84, 95% CI: 1.12, 3.06); and (5) if they had more years of experience conducting grant-funded research (OR = 1.67 for every ten years of experience, 95% CI; 1.15, 2.45).

In terms of Diversity Supplement receipt, only one predictor was significant in a combined model: psychologists who mentored undergraduates were significantly less likely to receive a Diversity Supplement (OR = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.07, 0.94).

text.text: National Institutes of Health Diversity Supplements have been a funding mechanism through which psychologists can support minoritized trainees, improving diversity in the field's research workforce by improving equity in research funding.

Diversity Supplements appear well-suited to address the field's goals regarding workforce diversity (Akbar et al.https://paperpile.com/c/q2qUOa/Prxky+o9t0O 2022; Buchanan et al., 2021) , and are unique among programs promoting workforce diversity in that they provide financial assistance to support positions that would not otherwise exist (David et al., 2022; Gichane et al., 2025).

text.text: Despite this, Diversity Supplements have been vastly underutilized; recent research found that fewer than 5% of active R01 grants have ever received a Diversity Supplement (Hill et al., 2021).

text.text: Prior empirical research on the barriers and facilitators of Diversity Supplement utilization have suggested that a lack of awareness and institutional support constitute important barriers (Preis et al., 2020; Rubio et al., 2024; Travers et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Prior empirical research on the barriers and facilitators of Diversity Supplement utilization have suggested that a lack of awareness and institutional support constitute important barriers <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Preis et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Rubio et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Travers et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, these studies, which emerged from small working groups at specific institutions, are limited in their ability to speak to broad trends in Diversity Supplement utilization across the field.

The present study sought to investigate rates of Diversity Supplement utilization by psychologists, researcher characteristics that predicted Diversity Supplement application and receipt, and psychologist-reported barriers to application.
These results provide important insights regarding Diversity Supplement utilization and suggest ways to improve the utilization of this funding mechanism.

The present study found that less than half (40.1%) of surveyed psychologists (all of whom had received an NIH grant) had ever applied for a Diversity Supplement, echoing previous research finding that Diversity Supplements are rarely utilized across the health sciences (Hill et al., 2021 (Hill et al., , 2023)).
text.formatted: The present study found that less than half (40.1%) of surveyed psychologists (all of whom had received an NIH grant) had ever applied for a Diversity Supplement, echoing previous research finding that Diversity Supplements are rarely utilized across the health sciences <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Hill et al., 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Hill et al., , 2023))</ref>.

text.text: Notably, the proportion of PIs who had ever received a Diversity Supplement (32.8%) was larger than one might expect given the small number of active eligible grants that had received a Diversity Supplement in 2020 (https://paperpile.com/c/q2qUOa/T0CaX/?prefix=less%20than%205%25%2C%20per  Hill et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Notably, the proportion of PIs who had ever received a Diversity Supplement (32.8%) was larger than one might expect given the small number of active eligible grants that had received a Diversity Supplement in 2020 (<ref type="url" target="https://paperpile.com/c/q2qUOa/T0CaX/?prefix=less%20than%205%25%2C%20per">less than 5%, per</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Hill et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: A few potential explanations for this discrepancy warrant discussion.
First, this may suggest that PIs generally receive Diversity Supplements for only a minority of their NIH grants.
Second, it is possible that Diversity Supplements are more frequently awarded on non-R01 grants (the focus on Hill's research).

Third, this finding could reflect the continuation of the upwards trend in Diversity Supplement receipt observed by Hill (while fewer than 100 Diversity Supplements were granted to R01s in each year before 2014, 2020 saw more than 400).
Lastly, it could be that PIs who received Diversity Supplements were disproportionately likely to participate in our study (this is discussed below as a limitation).

Of note, the rates of psychologists who applied and received Diversity Supplements were similar to those of non-psychologists, suggesting that psychologists' under-utilization of this mechanism reflects this wider trend.

Psychologists with racially/ethnically minoritized identities (particularly Black non-Hispanic and Hispanic psychologists) were more likely to apply for Diversity Supplements, as were psychologists who were more advanced in their careers (full professors and those with more years of experience); it is possible that these PIs were more aware of Diversity Supplements, more motivated to pursue them, or (particularly in the case of Black non-Hispanic and Hispanic PIs) more likely to work with eligible trainees.
Notably, however, these psychologists were not necessarily more successful in their applications.

The only psychologist characteristic that predicted Diversity Supplement receipt was mentorship type; psychologists who mentored undergraduates were significantly less likely to apply for, and had less success in being awarded Diversity Supplements.

The latter finding may owe to NIH preferences regarding applicants; it has been observed that "most awards appear to be granted to those at the higher end of the educational spectrum, commonly those seeking a PhD, post-doctoral fellowship, or junior faculty" (David et al., 2022).

text.text: Why do so few psychologists apply for Diversity Supplements?
We surveyed psychologists about a number of barriers, drawn from an array of Theoretical Domains Framework construct (e.g., knowledge, intentions, beliefs about consequences).
Ultimately, the most commonly cited barrier in our sample was a lack of qualifying mentees, endorsed by 34.8% of psychologists.

Trainees qualify for Diversity Supplements when they come from underrepresented groups including "racial and ethnic minorities, persons with disabilities and individuals from economically and educationally disadvantaged backgrounds that have inhibited their ability to pursue a career in health-related research" (https://paperpile.com/c/q2qUOa/jz0WQ.
text.formatted: Trainees qualify for Diversity Supplements when they come from underrepresented groups including "racial and ethnic minorities, persons with disabilities and individuals from economically and educationally disadvantaged backgrounds that have inhibited their ability to pursue a career in health-related research" (<ref type="url" target="https://paperpile.com/c/q2qUOa/jz0WQ">National Institutes of Health, 2024a)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, this barrier may reflect a lack of such trainees in the field of psychology in general (a limitation in the environmental context and resources that shape Diversity Supplement application); while psychology trainees have become more racially and ethnically diverse in recent years, rates still lag behind the general U.S. population (Stamm et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Thus, this barrier may reflect a lack of such trainees in the field of psychology in general (a limitation in the environmental context and resources that shape Diversity Supplement application); while psychology trainees have become more racially and ethnically diverse in recent years, rates still lag behind the general U.S. population <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Stamm et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, a lack of eligible trainees in the field may only be part of the problem; there are likely many trainees who would be eligible to be supported by a Diversity Supplement, but do not belong to labs that are actively seeking or receiving NIH funding.

Ultimately, a failure to effectively match mentees with PIs could be an important limiting factor in the utilization of Diversity Supplements; a strong match between trainee and mentor has been identified as an important factor in the success of the Diversity Supplement application, as well as of the research endeavor (David et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Ultimately, a failure to effectively match mentees with PIs could be an important limiting factor in the utilization of Diversity Supplements; a strong match between trainee and mentor has been identified as an important factor in the success of the Diversity Supplement application, as well as of the research endeavor <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(David et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Additional barriers reflected a lack of knowledge regarding Diversity Supplements; 22.6% of psychologists reported that they were unfamiliar with Diversity Supplement eligibility criteria, 12.8% reported being unfamiliar with the process of applying, and 9.0% reported being unfamiliar with the mechanism altogether.
These results suggest that there is more work to be done to educate psychological researchers about Diversity Supplements (Preis et al., 2020; Rubio et al., 2024).
text.formatted: These results suggest that there is more work to be done to educate psychological researchers about Diversity Supplements <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Preis et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Rubio et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These knowledge-related barriers reflect limitations in researchers' psychological capability, rather than a lack of interest or motivation.

Indeed, very few psychologists reported that a lack of interest, time, or incentives contributed to them not pursuing Diversity Supplements, which seems to indicate that applications would increase if there was greater clarity regarding the process and/or support helping identify eligible mentees.
Limitations.
Our survey was intentionally brief in order to minimize participant burden and maximize response rates.
However, this limits our ability to speak to certain factors that may influence Diversity Supplement utilization.

These include mentee demographic characteristics; while analyses found that many respondents cited a "lack of qualifying mentees," without With regards to our second research question ("What psychologist characteristics predict Diversity Supplement application and receipt?"), our findings may be limited by the fact that only some (79.8%) respondents opted into providing demographic information.
This could lead to bias in our findings if the relationship between demographic characteristics and Diversity Supplement application/receipt differs between respondents and nonrespondents.
Notably, analyses did find that nonrespondents were more likely to have applied for Diversity Supplements.
A final limitation may be our survey's generalizability to the larger population of NIH-supported PIs.

text.text: Per RePORT, PIs on research grants in 2018 (the midpoint of our sample, which included PIs funded between 2014 and 2022) were 74.0% White (including Hispanic), 22.0% Asian, 5.3% Hispanic, and 2.3% Black; in our sample, 74.6% of participants who provided race/ethnicity data were White non-Hispanic, 9.6% were Asian, 7.7% were Hispanic, and 3.1% were Black.
In terms of gender, 34.9% of NIH-funded PIs in 2018 were women, while 59.0% of respondents who provided gender data were women.
Thus, our survey may over-represent women, and under-represent Asian respondents, relative to the larger population of NIH-funded PIs on research grants in the study period.

It is also possible that PIs who were already familiar with Diversity Supplements were more likely to respond to our survey, which could bias our estimates of how many PIs have applied for or received Diversity Supplements upwards.
Recommendations.

The authors make two primary recommendations in line with our findings, which may support the utilization of NIH Diversity Supplements (should they be reinstated) or of similar funding mechanisms in the future.

First, considering that more than a third of psychologist respondents cited a lack of qualifying mentees as a barrier to applying, the authors recommend the creation of an informal matching system whereby interested trainees from underrepresented groups can be matched to NIH-supported mentors.
Such a system would directly enhance researchers' opportunity to apply by addressing structural barriers to identifying eligible mentees.
A matching system could connect trainees to potential mentors based on availability, interest, and other factors pertinent to the proposed work (e.g., skills, prior experience, and location).

A match could occur before the PI has developed a proposal for Diversity Supplement-supported research (and the PI could work with the matched trainee to develop a proposal), or a PI could have a proposal in mind that they would like to find a trainee for.
Such a system could exist between or within institutions.
For example, the University of Pittsburgh has found success creating their own matching system for researchers and interested mentees (Rubio et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For example, the University of Pittsburgh has found success creating their own matching system for researchers and interested mentees <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Rubio et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A similar system could be replicated at other institutions or scaled up to operate across institutions (notably, Diversity Supplements do not require that the trainee and PI be at the same institution).

Second, considering that many psychologists reported a lack of knowledge regarding Diversity Supplements, the authors recommend the creation or expansion of awareness campaigns regarding Diversity Supplements.

Such campaigns would strengthen researchers' capability by increasing familiarity with eligibility criteria and application procedures, and may also reinforce motivation by highlighting the scientific, professional, and equity-related benefits of pursuing these awards.
Moreover, advertisements and communications should clearly articulate (a) who is eligible to receive a Diversity Supplement and (b) how one can apply for a Diversity Supplement.

The responsibility of communicating with PIs about Diversity Supplements should be taken up by professional organizations, academic institutions that employ PIs, and by the NIH itself (which could share additional information about Diversity Supplements with grant recipients).
Conclusion.
Diversity Supplements have been underutilized as a tool for improving the diversity of the psychological workforce and for improving equity in research funding.
Survey responses indicated that although researchers are motivated to pursue diversity supplements, they have had limited perceived capability and opportunity to do so.

In order to capitalize on the potential of Diversity Supplements and similar funding support mechanisms to make a positive impact on workforce diversity the authors recommend that the field pursue additional avenues for education regarding Diversity Supplements (particularly with regards to eligibility criteria and the application process) and the creation of a match system that can be used to connect trainees from underrepresented groups to NIH-funded mentors.
